blocks.text: 55.1 Declinable Numbers

We have so far seen several numbers, such as quattuor ‘four’ and quīnque ‘five’. These are indeclinable, so that the same form is used regardless of the gender, number, or case of the items being counted: quattuor virī vēnērunt ‘four men came’, quattuor puellās vīdī ‘I saw four girls’. But the numbers ‘one’, ‘two’, and ‘three’ inflect: ‘one’ follows the pronominal declension like ipse, ‘three’ is a third-declension adjective, and ‘two’ is irregular (it is one of the few Latin remnants of the dual number, which was originally used when referring to two things, with the plural restricted to three or more things).
British Case Order
Ancient Case Order
‘One’ also has a plural; this is not common and inflects regularly: ūnī, ūnae, ūna, etc.
Translate:
duas oves amissas quaero.
duobus vel tribus pueris dona dedit.
rogavit num tres puellae adessent.
duobus gladiis se defendit.
argentum unius militis amissum est.
uno saxo magno hostem interfecit.
cum duabus sororibus hic maneamus.
rogaverunt num tria dona haberemus.
uni servo imperabo ut te iuvet, non duobus.
domus duorum vel trium agricolarum refectae sunt.
tres annos Carthagine manebimus.
duobus annis Londinio domum veniet.
cum tribus amicis advenit.
sit unum ius omnibus civibus.
Translate into Latin:
I shall free two or three slaves.
How many gifts do you have? – Three.
Within three years he will go to Athens.
Give that to one of the slaves.
The city is defended by two large walls.
Come (plural) with two or three girls.
How many sisters do you have, one or two?
The books of two girls have been found.
We stayed in Rome for two years.
I persuaded three men with one gift.
One of my friends has become a (personal) enemy.
When will your two brothers arrive?
55.2 Alius and Alter

Latin has two words for ‘other’: in most circumstances alius is used, but when ‘other’ means the other of two (usually ‘the other’ in English), alter is used. Both these words can be pronouns or adjectives; alius declines similarly to iste, and alter similarly to ipse.
British Case Order
Ancient Case Order
The genitive of alter, alterīus, is often used instead of alīus as genitive singular of alius.
Examples:
quid dīxit alter? ‘What did the other man say?’
quid dīcunt aliī? ‘What are the others saying?’
When two forms of alius occur together, they often mean ‘one . . . another’ or, in the plural, ‘some . . . others’; similarly two forms of alter can mean ‘one . . . the other’.
aliī volunt, aliī nōlunt. ‘Some want (it, and) others do not (want it).’
alter puer magnus est, alter parvus. ‘One boy (of the two) is big, the other little.’
But if two forms of alius are in different genders, numbers, or cases, each must be translated twice in English; usually one can also translate this construction with ‘different’ and a plural.

alius aliam amat. ‘One man loves one woman, and another loves another woman.’ / ‘Different men love different women.’ aliī alia dīxērunt. ‘Some people said some things, and others said other things.’ / ‘Different people said different things.’

duo libri mihi legendi sunt; alter longior est, alter brevior.
rogaverunt unde aliae puellae venissent.
alii gladiis se defendebant, alii saxis.
alii alia fecerunt.
harum duarum artium altera facilis est, altera difficilis.
tria dona accepi, quorum unum bonum est et alia mala.
alii pueri a magistro docentur, alii domi manent.
illo die alius aliud vidit.
illum Athenis vidi, alios Corinthi.
hoc nescio, sed multa alia scio.
quaesivit ubi alias puellas vidissemus.
aliae alia emerunt.
nihil aliud invenire poteram.
pecunia mea inventa est, sed pecunia omnium aliorum amissa est.
alter magister nunc adest, alter duobus diebus veniet.
rogaverunt num alios servos liberaturus essem.
nescivit quando adventuri essent alii.
aliae alia invenerunt.
duo servi sumus; dominus alterius bonus est, alterius malus.
si alii hostes venissent, nostri victi essent.
horum duorum alter nos verbis iuvit, alter factis.
alii poetae versus pessimos scribunt, sed ego versus optimos.
hic servus doctissimus est, sed alii nihil sciunt.
alia oppida moenibus defenduntur, sed nostrum nulla habet.
tres equi mortui sunt, sed alii valent.
Translate into Latin:
I have two good horses; the others are very bad.
This man has said nothing, but the other will ask where we found these three books.
One of you will be allowed to depart; the others must wait here.
The others asked whether
I myself will give money to one boy; you will have to give money to the others.
I love one of my two brothers, but I cannot love the other.
He said nothing else (= other), but he knows more.
The other men do not know how many names Roman men had.
had given gifts to the three 10 I can persuade the other men sisters. with gifts, but those two will not
The slaves of three citizens have accept money. fled, but the slaves of the others have remained.
The other man asked whether I had fought with two swords or with one.
55.3 Reading Practice
1 Livy, Ab urbe condita 1.21.6: comparison of two early kings of Rome, Romulus and Numa (written in the first century bc about a much earlier and partly mythical period).

Ita duo deinceps reges, alius alia via, ille bello hic pace, civitatem auxerunt. Romulus septem et triginta regnavit annos, Numa tres et quadraginta. cum valida tum temperata et belli et pacis artibus erat civitas.
Vocabulary

rows: augeō, augēre, auxī, auctum ‘cause to grow’
2 St Augustine, Confessions 1.13 (adapted): as a child, the saint preferred Virgil to mathematics, an opinion he later considered sinful (fourth century ad).

Peccabam ergo puer, cum illa inania his utilioribus amore praeponerem – vel potius haec oderam, illa amabam. iam vero ‘unum et unum sunt duo, duo et duo sunt quattuor’ odiosa cantio mihi erat, et dulcissima erant spectacula vanitatis: equus ligneus plenus armatis, et Troiae incendium, atque ipsius umbra Creusae.

dead wife, who appears as a ghost

unum oculum Thais non habet, ille duos.
